# How to keep up with AI in 2026 without drowning: 8 ways that actually work

Six new models a week. A thousand "this changes everything" threads a day. Two newsletters you keep
meaning to read and never do. Keeping up with AI in 2026 isn't a knowledge problem anymore — it's a
**filtering** problem.

I've tried most of the ways to stay current. Here are the eight that actually hold up, roughly from
"lowest effort" to "most effort," with the honest trade-offs.

## 1. A dedicated AI news app (lowest effort)

The newsletter graveyard is real — you subscribe, three land in Promotions, you declare bankruptcy. An
app you open for 30 seconds beats an inbox you avoid.

I've been using [a 30-second AI news reader](https://kapyn.app) called **Kapyn**. It pulls from ~30
primary sources (the labs' own blogs, TechCrunch, The Verge, Hacker News, arXiv-adjacent), uses AI to
distill each story to 2–3 calm sentences, and you swipe through them like Inshorts. No hype, no paywall.
It also has a side-by-side [AI model comparison](https://kapyn.app/compare) and a glossary that ties each
concept to the latest news. Good for the "I have 5 minutes, what actually happened" use case.

**Trade-off:** great for breadth and speed; not where you go for deep 4,000-word analysis.

## 2. One high-signal newsletter (not five)

Pick **one** and actually read it. The Rundown and TLDR AI are the usual picks. The mistake is
subscribing to six — you read none. One newsletter, read consistently, beats a folder of unread ones.

**Trade-off:** daily cadence means you're always a little behind on breaking stuff.

## 3. Hacker News, filtered

HN front page + the comments is still the best signal-per-minute on the internet for technical AI news —
*if* you filter. Sort by points, skip the drama threads. The comments often matter more than the article.

**Trade-off:** heavy dev skew; you'll miss the product/business side.

## 4. Two or three primary sources directly

If you only care about frontier models, just read the source: the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind
blogs. Zero middlemen, zero spin.

**Trade-off:** you only see what those three ship — you miss the wider ecosystem.

## 5. A tight X / Twitter list

Not your timeline — a **curated list** of 20–30 researchers and builders. The algorithm feed will bury
you; a list won't.

**Trade-off:** high noise-to-signal unless you prune the list ruthlessly.

## 6. r/LocalLLaMA and r/MachineLearning

The best place to learn what practitioners *actually* think — which models hold up in production, which
frameworks over-promise. The honest counterweight to launch-day hype.

**Trade-off:** Reddit is a time sink; go in with a question, not to browse.

## 7. Podcasts for the "why," not the "what"

Podcasts are terrible for breaking news (too slow) and great for context. Use them for the deeper "why
does this matter" while you walk or commute — not to find out what shipped.

## 8. Just ask a model

Genuinely underrated: ask Claude or ChatGPT "what were the biggest AI developments this week?" It won't be
perfectly current, but for a quick catch-up after a busy week it's fine.

**Trade-off:** knowledge cutoffs and hallucinated dates — verify anything that matters.

---

## The honest recommendation

Most people don't need all eight. They need **one fast daily input** for breadth (an app or one
newsletter) plus **one deep input** for context (HN, a subreddit, or a podcast). That's it. The people
who "keep up with AI" effortlessly aren't reading more — they've just picked a system and stuck to it.

If you want the fast daily input, [Kapyn](https://kapyn.app) is free and takes 30 seconds. If you want to
go deep, pick HN or r/LocalLLaMA. Either way — pick a system, delete the other six tabs, and stop feeling
behind.

*What's your setup? Curious what actually works for people who ship.*
